Let
\[
T_n=\dim F(\mathbb F_5^n)=\frac{11}{6}n^2(n^2-1),
\]
and
\[
b_n=\frac{n(n-2)(n-1)(n+1)}8,\qquad
c_n=\frac{n^2(n^2-1)}{12}.
\]
Then the answer is
\[
\boxed{
\left(R_n^{(1)},N_n^{(1)},R_n^{(2)},N_n^{(2)}\right)=
\begin{cases}
\left(T_n-b_n,\ 3100,\ T_n-c_n,\ 120\right),& n=4,5,\\[2mm]
\left(2205,\ 3220,\ 2100,\ 782625\right),& n=6,\\[2mm]
\left(T_n-c_n,\ 120,\ T_n-b_n,\ 3100\right),& n\ge 7.
\end{cases}}
\]

Here is the derivation.

Since \(5\nmid 24\), \(\mathbb F_5[S_4]\) is semisimple. The idempotent \(e\) removes exactly the trivial and sign blocks. The remaining simple \(S_4\)-modules have dimensions
\[
3,\quad 3,\quad 2
\]
corresponding to partitions \((31),(211),(22)\). For \(n\ge4\), Schur-Weyl independence gives
\[
G(\mathbb F_5^n)\cong
S_{31}(\mathbb F_5^n)\otimes M_{31}
\oplus
S_{211}(\mathbb F_5^n)\otimes M_{211}
\oplus
S_{22}(\mathbb F_5^n)\otimes M_{22}.
\]
The Schur dimensions are
\[
a_n=\frac{n(n-1)(n+1)(n+2)}8,\quad
b_n=\frac{n(n-2)(n-1)(n+1)}8,\quad
c_n=\frac{n^2(n^2-1)}{12}.
\]
Thus
\[
\dim F=2(3a_n+3b_n+2c_n)=\frac{11}{6}n^2(n^2-1)=T_n.
\]

The adjoint involution makes each doubled multiplicity space a hyperbolic orthogonal space of dimension \(2d\), where \(d=3,3,2\). A hyperbolically self-dual idempotent is exactly orthogonal projection onto a nondegenerate subspace. Therefore, if \(Q=I-E\), the rank deficit of \(E\) is the rank of \(Q\), weighted by \(a_n,b_n,c_n\).

For a split hyperbolic space of dimension \(2d\) over \(\mathbb F_5\), the number of nondegenerate lines is
\[
5^{d-1}(5^d-1).
\]
So for \(d=3\) this is
\[
5^2(125-1)=3100,
\]
and for \(d=2\) this is
\[
5(25-1)=120.
\]

Now compare weights:
\[
a_n>b_n,\qquad a_n>c_n,
\]
and
\[
c_n-b_n=\frac{n(n-1)(n+1)(6-n)}{24}.
\]
Hence \(b_n<c_n\) for \(n=4,5\), \(b_n=c_n\) for \(n=6\), and \(c_n<b_n\) for \(n\ge7\). That gives the largest proper ranks except at \(n=6\) immediately.

For \(n=6\), \(b_6=c_6=105\), \(a_6=210\), \(T_6=2310\). The largest proper rank is
\[
2310-105=2205,
\]
attained by a nondegenerate line in either the \(d=3\) \(b\)-block or the \(d=2\) \(c\)-block, so
\[
N_6^{(1)}=3100+120=3220.
\]
The second deficit is \(210\). It can occur as:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{one line in the }a\text{-block}: &&3100,\\
&\text{a rank-2 nondegenerate subspace in the }b\text{-block}: &&406875,\\
&\text{a rank-2 nondegenerate subspace in the }c\text{-block}: &&650,\\
&\text{one line in each of the }b,c\text{ blocks}: &&3100\cdot120.
\end{aligned}
\]
The rank-2 counts come from counting nondegenerate planes in split orthogonal spaces over \(\mathbb F_5\). Thus
\[
N_6^{(2)}
=3100+406875+650+3100\cdot120
=782625.
\]
So
\[
R_6^{(2)}=2310-210=2100.
\]

This proves the stated piecewise quadruple.
